title: Stage 2: Features
summary: Turn raw columns into model inputs: age from year built, one-hot neighbourhoods, and a matrix with an intercept column.

steps.title: Stage 2: features
body: A linear model computes `price ≈ b0 + b1·x1 + b2·x2 + ...`. Every input must be a **number**, and the more directly it expresses the idea, the better:
- `age = 2024 - year_built` reads better than a year (and its coefficient means "per year older").
- `neighbourhood` is a category. **One-hot encode** it: one 0/1 column per neighbourhood.

`drop_first=True` leaves out one neighbourhood (`Central`, the first alphabetically). It becomes the **reference**: the other columns mean "compared with Central". Keeping all three alongside an intercept would make the columns add up to the intercept column, and the model could not tell them apart.

steps.explain: Categories are sorted; `Central` is dropped. A `Central` house is the row of zeros.

steps.prompt: Why keep the original `df` unchanged in `add_features`?
options: So you can rerun the pipeline and try other features from the same raw data
It makes the model more accurate

steps.title: Add features
prompt: Add a module-level list and a function:

`add_features(df)` returns a **new** DataFrame with `age = 2024 - year_built`, the neighbourhood one-hot encoded (`prefix="nb"`, `drop_first=True`, `dtype=int`), and `year_built` and `neighbourhood` removed. Column order: `sqm, bedrooms, price, age, nb_Hilltop, nb_Riverside`.

FEATURES = ["sqm", "bedrooms", "age", "nb_Hilltop", "nb_Riverside"]


def add_features(df):
    out = df.copy()
    out["age"] = 2024 - out["year_built"]
    dummies = pd.get_dummies(out["neighbourhood"], prefix="nb", drop_first=True, dtype=int)
